query: For additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components, what single intervention could improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity while reducing fabrication-induced defects? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the current fabrication baseline, defines the processing and application conditions under which it should hold, identifies supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a minor addition of chromium (around 4–5 at%) into the base high-entropy alloy feedstock will improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity of additively manufactured components by promoting the formation of a fine, reticulated secondary phase (Laves phase) that enhances solid solution hardening and crack resistance, thus reducing fabrication-induced defects.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured high-entropy alloy components based on a baseline composition similar to HfMoTaTiZr, which in their as-built state exhibit typical dimensional distortions and mechanical weaknesses owing to rapid solidification and inherent processing defects.
generation.intervention: Slight alloying modification by adding approximately 4–5 at% Cr to the base composition prior to processing.
generation.conditions: The intervention is applied during the feedstock formulation for additive manufacturing (e.g., laser powder bed fusion or selective laser melting) under inert atmosphere conditions, with process parameters optimized for near-equilibrium microstructure formation.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a minor Laves phase within the predominantly BCC microstructure, with indications of reduced lattice parameters and a reticulated distribution at grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The added Cr dissolves into the BCC phase causing lattice distortion (solid solution hardening) while also promoting the controlled nucleation of a fine Laves phase. This dual mechanism is expected to offset rapid thermal gradients and residual stresses during AM processing, thereby reducing defect formation and enhancing resistance to crack propagation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved dimensional precision (through reduced distortion and residual stresses) and enhanced mechanical integrity (with increases in hardness, yield strength, and fracture toughness) relative to components produced from the unmodified alloy. The magnitude of these improvements is expected to be in a similar order of enhancement observed in vacuum arc–melted samples (e.g., near 50–60% improvement in hardness) but with some uncertainty regarding absolute values under AM conditions.
generation.baseline: Components manufactured from the baseline HfMoTaTiZr alloy (without Cr addition) that exhibit known issues with fabrication-induced defects and less optimal mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold under AM conditions where the cooling rates and thermal gradients allow for controlled secondary phase formation; extreme processing conditions that lead to vastly different microstructures may not yield the same benefits.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty related to transferring the alloy design insights from vacuum arc melting studies to additive manufacturing processes, especially given differing thermal histories and potential phase evolution under rapid solidification in AM.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy powders: one for the baseline HfMoTaTiZr composition and one modified with 4–5 at% Cr. Fabricate identical component geometries using the same additive manufacturing process (e.g., laser powder bed fusion) and identical processing parameters. Post-fabrication, conduct a comparative microstructural analysis (using SEM, EBSD, and XRD) and assess dimensional accuracy using high-resolution metrology. Mechanical testing (e.g., hardness, compression/tensile tests, and fracture toughness measurements) should be carried out on both sets.
measurements: Dimensional deviation measurements (e.g., using optical or X-ray methods)
Phase composition and microstructure via XRD and electron microscopy
Mechanical property tests: hardness, yield strength, and fracture toughness
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis would be falsified if the Cr-modified components do not show statistically significant improvements in both dimensional precision and mechanical performance (i.e., no meaningful reduction in fabrication-induced defects, similar or inferior mechanical properties, or an absence of the expected Laves phase formation) when compared to the baseline components.

cited_evidence.text: Paper card. Question: How does the addition of Cr to the HfMoTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy affect its phase composition, microstructure, and room-temperature mechanical properties, specifically regarding the synergy between strength and ductility?. System: HfMoTaTiZr (30.0 at% Hf, 16.1 at% Mo, 30.4 at% Ta, 8.1 at% Ti, 15.4 at% Zr) and HfMoTaTiZrCr0.5 (28.8 at% Hf, 15.5 at% Mo, 29.1 at% Ta, 7.7 at% Ti, 14.7 at% Zr, 4.2 at% Cr). Processing: Vacuum arc melting in an inert gas atmosphere; ingots re-melted at least 5 times to improve chemical homogeneity; weight loss did not exceed 0.5 wt%. Test conditions: Room temperature; Vickers hardness with 0.3 kg load and 15 s dwelling time; compression tests on cylindrical samples (3 mm diameter, 6 mm height) at a ram speed of 0.008 mm s−1 (strain rate 0.001/s).
